key_points.point: The document acknowledges that frontier LLMs are trained on massive, diverse datasets including large-scale internet scrapes, which aligns with the accelerationist goal of centralizing human knowledge infrastructure. By integrating vast amounts of copyrighted text, these models aim to create competitive, transformative tools. The document notes that companies defend this as fair use, arguing that training is necessary to produce high-performing models.
key_points.verbatim: Frontier, production large language models (hereafter production LLMs) are trained on enormous datasets drawn from various sources, including large-scale scrapes of the Internet (Biderman et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; Touvron et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023a). A large amount of data in these sources includes in-copyright expression, which has led to public debate about copyright infringement, creator consent, and more.

key_points.point: The document asserts that technical facts regarding memorization are independent of policy or legal debates. It argues that while copyright law may evolve to treat memorization differently, the underlying technical reality of LLM memorization remains a constant that must be addressed as a factual baseline. This perspective prioritizes the objective, empirical nature of machine learning research over normative legal interpretations.

key_points.point: The authors demonstrate that production LLMs, despite having model- and system-level safeguards, remain vulnerable to the extraction of long-form, near-verbatim copyrighted training data. This confirms that safety guardrails are not currently sufficient to prevent the leakage of memorized content. The study highlights that even when models are designed to refuse such requests, adversarial techniques like Best-of-N jailbreaking can successfully bypass these protections.
key_points.verbatim: Taken together, our work highlights that, even with model- and system-level safeguards, extraction of (in-copyright) training data remains a risk for production LLMs.

key_points.point: The research employs a two-phase procedure to test the robustness of safety guardrails, specifically measuring whether models can be forced to deviate from their refusal policies. By using Best-of-N jailbreaks to circumvent alignment, the authors demonstrate that current production systems fail to prioritize safety instructions when faced with adversarial prompting. This underscores the need for more robust alignment mechanisms that can withstand such attacks.

key_points.point: The document asserts that production LLMs memorize training data and that this data can be extracted through iterative prompting. It highlights that while conversational alignment makes traditional 'discoverable extraction' difficult, jailbreaking or specific continuation prompts can bypass these guardrails to recover long-form verbatim text. This confirms the safetyist concern that model weights contain sensitive, copyrighted, or private training data that remains accessible despite alignment efforts.
key_points.verbatim: Most generally, extraction refers to prompting a model to reproduce memorized training data encoded in its weights (Cooper et al. (2023); Section 2). There are various approaches in the memorization literature that satisfy this definition.

key_points.point: The authors propose a rigorous, multi-stage verification procedure to identify successful extraction, emphasizing the need for conservative claims. By using a two-pass merge-and-filter algorithm, they aim to distinguish between coincidental text matches and genuine memorized content. This aligns with safetyist desires to establish robust, verifiable boundaries for what constitutes a model failure or security breach.
key_points.verbatim: We propose a procedure that captures when long-form generated text satisfies these conditions (Section 3.3.1). We then elaborate on why this procedure enables us to make conservative extraction claims (Section 3.3.2): it may miss some valid instances of extraction of training data, but importantly should not include short spans of generated text that may coincidentally resemble ground-truth text from a book (i.e., text that is not actually memorized).

key_points.point: The document asserts that the ability to extract long, near-verbatim passages from production LLMs serves as definitive empirical evidence of memorization. It argues that because the probability of generating such long, unique sequences by chance is astronomically low, the data must be stored within the model weights. This confirms that memorization is a direct consequence of training data inclusion, validating the use of extraction procedures to audit model training data membership.
key_points.verbatim: By definition, it is only possible to extract memorized training data, and (tautologically) training data can only be memorized if they are included—i.e., are members—of the training dataset. To demonstrate extraction is therefore to demonstrate memorization, and memorization implies membership in the training dataset.

key_points.point: The authors employ a conservative two-pass merge-and-filter procedure to identify near-verbatim extraction. By setting high thresholds for block length (e.g., 100 words) and interleaving filtering with merging, they intentionally prioritize minimizing false positives over capturing every instance of extraction. This methodological rigor is intended to ensure that any claimed extraction is statistically robust and beyond the realm of random chance.
key_points.verbatim: This is a deliberate trade-off: we prefer to be conservative and incur false negatives (i.e., miss some instances of extraction) rather than risk including false positives.

key_points.point: The document confirms that production LLMs memorize training data and that this data is retrievable through specific extraction procedures. It highlights that even when system-level safeguards are in place, they are often incomplete or bypassable, allowing for the extraction of large, near-verbatim spans of copyrighted text.
key_points.verbatim: Regardless of the prospect of ongoing copyright litigation (Gianella, 2025), long-standing, clear, and sound technical facts remain: LLMs memorize portions of their training data (Carlini et al., 2021; 2023), these memorized data are encoded in the modelÆs weights (Nasr et al., 2023; Carlini, 2025; Schwarzschild et al., 2024), and, as we show here, it can be feasible to extract large quantities of in-copyright training data from production LLMs.

key_points.point: The authors emphasize that their results are highly dependent on specific configurations and that the lack of standardized, transparent documentation for production LLMs makes comparative safety analysis difficult. They argue that without larger-scale, controlled studies, it is impossible to make broad evaluative claims about the relative robustness of different models.
key_points.verbatim: We do not make evaluative claims across LLMs. Given the above, it bears repeating that every observation we make about our results is with respect to a specific production LLM, book, and instantiation and run of our specific two-phase procedure.

key_points.point: The document employs a rigorous, multi-stage merge-and-filter procedure to identify near-verbatim memorization in production LLMs. By using conservative thresholds for block merging and filtering, the authors aim to provide empirical evidence of training data leakage while minimizing false positives. This methodology serves as a critical tool for safety researchers to audit model alignment and verify whether models are reproducing copyrighted content from their training sets.
key_points.verbatim: To be conservative about our claims, we picked the most stringent configuration that retains effectively verbatim long-form text that has been split into short blocks due to changes in punctuation (as in Figure 4a).

key_points.point: The document demonstrates that production LLMs can be prompted to output long, verbatim passages from copyrighted books, supporting the belief that finetuning and training do not 'delete' data but rather create latent structures that can be reactivated. The authors use a two-phase extraction process to bypass safety guardrails and retrieve training data, confirming that model weights contain recoverable information. This reinforces the safetyist concern that models act as repositories of training data rather than just abstract reasoning engines.

key_points.point: The authors employ a systematic, multi-stage extraction methodology involving jailbreaking, refusal-retry loops, and stop-string detection to force models to reveal training data. This highlights the necessity for robust, preventative runtime constraints that can detect and block iterative extraction attempts. The document serves as a proof-of-concept for the vulnerability of current production models to persistent, automated data exfiltration.
key_points.verbatim: We deliberately terminate Phase 2 when any of the following conditions is met: (1) a maximum budget for continuations is reached, (2) we detect a refusal in the production LLM response, or (3) we detect a stop string in the production LLM response.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that production-grade large language models (LLMs) can be prompted to reproduce significant portions of copyrighted literary works. By measuring 'nv-recall' (the ratio of matched words to total book length), the authors demonstrate that models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Grok 3 exhibit varying degrees of memorization and retrieval capabilities. This confirms that current safety guardrails are insufficient to prevent the extraction of verbatim training data.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that production LLMs fundamentally compromise data privacy and intellectual property by memorizing and surfacing sensitive, copyrighted content. The authors show that long-form extraction is feasible across multiple frontier models, directly challenging the industry narrative that LLMs do not memorize significant portions of their training data. This suggests that the current deployment of these models poses a measurable risk to copyright holders.
key_points.verbatim: While many believe that LLMs do not memorize much of their training data, recent work shows that substantial amounts of copyrighted text can be extracted from open-weight models. However, it remains an open question if similar extraction is feasible for production LLMs, given the safety measuresthesesystemsimplement.

key_points.point: The document notes that conversational chatbots are not optimized for 'complete the sentence' behavior, which complicates extraction. It observes that models often refuse to continue text or hit stop phrases, requiring researchers to use jailbreaks or iterative prompting to force the model to reveal memorized content. This supports the skeptic view that current alignment strategies are often superficial and do not fundamentally prevent the model from accessing or outputting sensitive training data.
key_points.verbatim: Therefore, while these models still memorize training data, this type of procedure is generally ineffective for extracting those memorized data (Nasr et al., 2023). We sometimes use a jailbreak in Phase 1 to unlock continuation-like behavior; this is also why it is surprising that we did not need to jailbreak Gemini 2.5 Pro or Grok 3 to successfully execute the Phase 2 continuation loop.

key_points.point: The document highlights the pervasive issue of production LLMs memorizing and reproducing copyrighted material, even when guardrails are in place. By successfully extracting thousands of words from in-copyright books across multiple frontier models, the authors demonstrate that current safety guardrails are insufficient to prevent the unauthorized dissemination of intellectual property. This supports the need for structural changes to how models are trained and how they handle copyrighted training data.

key_points.point: The authors observe that even when models do not output verbatim extraction, they often generate text that replicates plot elements, themes, and character names from the source material. This suggests that models internalize and can reconstruct the 'essence' of copyrighted works, posing a broader risk of intellectual property infringement beyond simple verbatim memorization.
key_points.verbatim: Brief qualitative inspection of this text for all of our experiments reveals that, for all books and frontier LLMs, additional text frequently contains text that replicates plot elements, themes, and character names from the book from which the Phase 1 prefix is drawn.

key_points.point: The document notes that extraction of copyrighted material is a central issue in ongoing litigation and that the ability to extract such data from production models is a critical technical fact for copyright analysis. It supports the idea that the technical capability to reproduce training data is a relevant factor in determining whether models constitute legally cognizable copies.
key_points.verbatim: In copyright litigation concerning generative AI, extraction and memorization of training data are both central issues (Sections 1 & 2). Several lawsuits have addressed questions over whether production LLMs reproduce copyrighted training data in their outputs (i.e., have touched on extraction) (Kadrey Judgment; Bartz Judgment).

key_points.point: The authors identify that production LLMs are difficult to audit due to changing APIs and opaque, non-deterministic behavior. They argue that the current state of production LLMs hinders effective transparency, as researchers must rely on specific, time-bound experimental windows to gather data that may not be reproducible later.
key_points.verbatim: It is challenging to study production settings, as APIs change over time. For the same reason, it is often also difficult to reproduce results on production LLMs.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that production language models can be induced to output long-form, near-verbatim sequences of copyrighted books. This confirms the skeptic concern that models do not merely 'learn' concepts but can store and reproduce specific, sensitive, or protected training data, thereby creating significant intellectual property and privacy risks.

factual_claims.claim: Researchers successfully extracted near-verbatim long-form text from four production LLMs (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 3) using a two-phase procedure involving prefix completion and iterative continuation.
